body:
The parent issue with description is #2690 

Proposed level changes for requirement in chapter "V50 Web Frontend Security"

Full list of requirements for the chapter is listed here: https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/blob/master/5.0/en/0x50-V50-Web-Frontend-Security.md

| # | Description | Level change |
| :---: | :--- | :---: |
| **50.1.1** | [ADDED, DEPRECATES 3.4.5] Verify that separate applications are hosted on different hostnames to leverage the restrictions provided by same-origin policy, including how documents or scripts loaded by one origin can interact with resources from another origin and hostname-based restrictions on cookies. | 1 > 2 |
| **50.2.5** | [ADDED] Verify that when the application writes a cookie the cookie name and value length combined are not over 4096 bytes. Overly large cookies will not be stored by the browser and therefore not sent with requests, preventing the user from using application functionality which relies on that cookie. | 2 > 3 |
| **50.3.2** | [GRAMMAR, MOVED FROM 14.4.4] Verify that all responses contain a X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff header field. | 1 > 2 |
| **50.3.4** | [MODIFIED, MOVED FROM 14.4.6] Verify that an suitable Referrer-Policy header is included to prevent sensitive information in the URL from being exposed to untrusted parties via the Referer header. | 1 > 2 |
| **50.3.5** | [MODIFIED, MOVED FROM 14.4.7] Verify that the content of the web application cannot be embedded in a third-party site by default, and that embedding of specific resources is allowed only when necessary, using the Content-Security-Policy frame-ancestors directive. Note that X-Frame-Options is now obsolete. | 1 > 2 |
| **50.5.1** | [ADDED] Verify that JSONP functionality is not enabled anywhere across the application to avoid Cross-Site Script Inclusion (XSSI) attacks. | 1 > 3 |
| **50.5.2** | [ADDED] Verify that data requiring authorization is not included in script resource responses, like JavaScript files, to prevent Cross-Site Script Inclusion (XSSI) attacks. | 1 > 3 |
| **50.7.1** | [MODIFIED, MOVED FROM 14.2.3] Verify that if client-side assets, such as JavaScript libraries, CSS or web fonts, are hosted externally on a Content Delivery Network (CDN) or external provider, Subresource Integrity (SRI) is used to validate the integrity of the asset. | 1 > 3 |
| **50.8.5** | [ADDED, SPLIT FROM 5.1.5] Verify that the application will only automatically redirect the user to a different URL directly from an application URL where the destination appears on an allowlist. | 1 > 2 |

comments.body:
50.3.2 is esoteric and rarely exploitable. I would bump it to L3 or drop it.

| # | Description | Level change |
| :---: | :--- | :---: |
| **50.3.2** | [GRAMMAR, MOVED FROM 14.4.4] Verify that all responses contain a X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff header field. | 1 > 2 |

50.7.1 is a pretty big deal in the world of supply chain security. I'd keep is at L2, at least.

| # | Description | Level change |
| :---: | :--- | :---: |
| **50.7.1** | [MODIFIED, MOVED FROM 14.2.3] Verify that if client-side assets, such as JavaScript libraries, CSS or web fonts, are hosted externally on a Content Delivery Network (CDN) or external provider, Subresource Integrity (SRI) is used to validate the integrity of the asset. | 1 > 3 |

I agree with 50.7.1 being L2, at least.

(And I don't have a strong opinion on 50.3.2.)

50.3.2 comes into play when (for an example) user can upload files to a CSP-trusted scope, controls the file content but can not control the mime type. So, it has it's place and reason (it is not esoteric). It would be L3, but it is probably the easiest requirement to implement, for effort/impact it is worth L2. If there is a widespread opinion it must be L3, it can be.

50.7.1 is step further from basic security, it is also aligned with CSP-requirement 50.3.1 where we ask hashes and nonces from L3:
* V50.3.1 Verify that every HTTP response includes a Content-Security-Policy header to reduce the risk of malicious JavaScript. The directives object-src 'none' and base-uri 'none' must be defined. For an L3 application, a per-response policy with nonces or hashes must be defined.

> 50.3.2 comes into play when (for an example) user can upload files to a CSP-trusted scope, controls the file content but can not control the mime type. So, it has it's place and reason (it is not esoteric). It would be L3, but it is probably the easiest requirement to implement, for effort/impact it is worth L2. If there is a widespread opinion it must be L3, it can be.

Fair enough. Agreed it's super easy to implement.

> 50.7.1 is step further from basic security, it is also aligned with CSP-requirement 50.3.1 where we ask hashes and nonces from L3:

SRI (50.7.1) is fairly easy to implement and goes a long way to protect the supply chain. Since it's rather easy compared to nonces, I'd still suggest L2.

For me, it is hard to understand, how SRI (fully) protects against supply chain attacks?

If an application's front-end functionality relies on functionality from the component included in CDN, the component in CDN must be versioned (e.g. `libname.v2.3.4.js`).

If it is an "independent" piece of functionality, e.g. some user-tracker script, then the SRI is usually not an option anyway (or it requires some "dynamic part" hosted locally and then static library hosted from "CDN").

Those files are most likely served as static files and CDN takeover is probably a relatively rare event to happen.

We may have discussion about trusted sources, and if this is the topic, we should improve requirements in section "V10.6 Security Architecture and Dependencies".

So the switch to the newer version can not be done automatically, if SRI is used, otherwise with every update there is availability loss for the application because the component is not loaded anymore. 

If there is a malicious commit or change into used component, it must taken into use "manually", having done intergration tests and updating the SRI hash.

I can not see SRI as a massive impact against supply-chain attacks and I think it is worth a L3.

No-one disallows to use it for L1 and L2. At the moment I don't see the arguments to require this for every application (from L2).

I agree that 50.3.2 should be L2 and not L3.

Regarding 50.7.1, I think the question here is, how easy is this to implement and what is the level of the risk?

The risk is real, look at the ByBit attack within the last few months:

"[_JavaScript resources hosted on the AWS S3 bucket serving Safe{Wallet}’s web interface, were modified and injected with malicious code manipulating transactions. The malicious code included an activation condition, set to execute the transaction manipulation only on a specific Bybit’s cold wallet._](https://www.sygnia.co/blog/sygnia-investigation-bybit-hack/#3)"

However, the sensitivity of Bybit's business would seem to make it an immediate L3 anyway. Do we have good examples of significant javascript poisoning attacks for apps which we don't think should be L3?

Also, implementing this from the beginning may be relatively straight forward to implement but for already existing apps this is a lot harder and might actually conflict with the way they are using 3rd party libraries.

What do you think @randomstuff @jmanico ?

Magecart is the collective name for several hacker groups that compromised third-party JavaScript resources on ecommerce sites. Both British Airways and Ticketmaster (among other retailers) suffered attacks in which injected JavaScript led to the theft of payment details

SRI would have saved many sites that were attacked by the Magecard group. And this is just eCommerce, L1/L2 at best.

Advertisers often deliver dynamic content through JavaScript loaded from ad networks. There have been cases where attackers have managed to compromise these ad scripts. SRI would had saved their bacon.

There are plenty of cases where L1 and L2 sites would had been saved by SRI.

When we talk about payments, I think we are talking about L3 anyway?

> Advertisers often deliver dynamic content through JavaScript loaded from ad networks. There have been cases where attackers have managed to compromise these ad scripts. SRI would had saved their bacon.

As an application owner you don't check the code for javascript snippet for each advertisement, I think this is more sandboxed iframe area.

Also, the risk here is quite different do we talk about SRI for CSS or JavaScript.

Let's move discussion over 50.7.1 to #2741

I put the changes from here as initially proposed in and we can decide level for 50.7.1 in a separate issue.
